name: Directional roughness
purpose: Roughness that has a direction. Brushed metal, hair, silk, vinyl, turned wood. Without it these are all grey plastic with a round highlight.

inputs.means: how stretched the highlight is; sign flips the axis
which way the micro-grooves run
turn the direction within the surface

outputs.means: two roughness values instead of one, along and across the grain

requires: a stable tangent frame per shading point
host_binding.binding_note: Direction must follow the PART, not the UV layout. UV-derived tangents break on curved parts and the highlight visibly snaps at seams — this is the most common wrong binding of this organ.

known_losses: A single tangent frame cannot express two grain directions crossing (woven metal mesh, brushed then polished).

fallback.do: stretch the roughness map along the grain direction
fallback.loses: correct highlight shape at glancing angles; crude but visibly better than isotropic

verify: Rotate a brushed disc 360 degrees under a fixed light. The highlight must stretch and sweep, not sit still as a round dot.

name: Micro-variation
purpose: Variation in roughness and colour that has nothing to do with the shape. The cheapest anti-CG move there is: uniform roughness IS the plastic look.

inputs.means: how much roughness wanders around its value
how much base colour wanders
size of the variation in real millimetres — pores are ~1.6, wood grain ~4, marble veining ~30
stretch the variation along the grain
how many scales of variation are layered

outputs.means: per-point offsets applied to roughness and base colour before shading

requires: a deterministic noise source keyed by object position, not screen position
host_binding.binding_note: MUST be object-space and deterministic, or the surface crawls when the camera moves and the same asset differs between renders. A seed belongs in the surface record so two renders of one asset match.

known_losses: Procedural breakup cannot express structure a real surface has for a reason (a scar, a weld, a scratch someone made). Those stay texture work.

fallback.when: host has no procedural noise in the shader
fallback.do: bake a tiling roughness-variation texture per material and multiply it in
fallback.loses: scale independence; a baked map tiles visibly on large surfaces

verify: Two spheres, identical except one with roughness_variation 0.15. The varied one should look like a thing and the flat one like a render. If you cannot tell them apart, it is not bound.
Render the same asset twice. The variation must be identical both times.

name: Clear coat
purpose: A second smooth layer over a rougher one. Car paint, varnish, lacquer, wet surfaces, eyes, sebum on skin.

inputs.means: how present the coat is; drive it with a map for wetness and sweat
roughness of the coat only, independent of the layer beneath
index of refraction of the coat
absorption in the coat, for tinted lacquers

outputs.means: a second specular lobe plus energy removed from the layer beneath

requires: a second specular evaluation per shading point
host_binding.binding_note: Wetness is a coat change, not an albedo change. Darkening base colour to fake wet is the classic mistake and it reads as dirt.

known_losses: Light bouncing between coat and base is usually approximated, so deep metallic paint is slightly under-saturated.

fallback.when: host has one specular lobe only
fallback.do: render a second pass of the same geometry, low roughness, additive, masked where the coat is
fallback.loses: energy conservation; record that the fallback was used

verify: A car-paint sphere must show two highlights at different sharpness. One highlight means the coat is not bound.

name: Thin-film iridescence
purpose: Colour that changes with viewing angle. Oil films, soap, beetle shells, tempered steel, fuel on water. Cheap, and instantly reads as not-plastic.

inputs.means: strength of the interference colour
film thickness in nanometres; this is what sets the hue
how much thickness wanders, which is what makes the colour swirl
index of refraction of the film

outputs.means: an angle-dependent tint applied to the specular lobe only

requires: view angle at the shading point
host_binding.binding_note: Tints the specular lobe only. Applying it to diffuse gives a metallic-paint look that is wrong but often shipped.

known_losses: Single-layer film only; real shells are stacked layers and are more saturated than this can express.

fallback.do: a view-angle-driven hue ramp on the specular tint
fallback.loses: physical hue ordering; looks decorative rather than material

verify: Rotate an iridescent sphere. The hue must sweep. If the colour is fixed, it is not bound.

name: Grazing-angle sheen
purpose: Retroreflective fuzz at glancing angles. Velvet, wool, dust on cloth, and the fine vellus hair that gives real faces a rim halo.

inputs.means: strength of the fuzz lobe
how tight the rim is; low is a sharp edge line, high is a broad glow
colour of the fibre tips, usually paler than the base

outputs.means: an additive lobe weighted toward grazing angles, energy-conserving against the diffuse term

requires: view and normal at the shading point
host_binding.binding_note: Cheapest organ in the set. Bind this first if you bind only one.

known_losses: Single-scatter only: deep pile fabric loses its inter-fibre bounce and reads slightly flat in shadow.

fallback.do: Fresnel-weighted additive term in the surface's own colour at weight ~0.2
fallback.loses: the tint being separable from the base colour

verify: A flat-lit velvet sphere must be nearly black in the centre and bright at the rim. If it looks like dark plastic with a highlight, sheen is not bound.

name: Subsurface transport
purpose: Lets light travel a short distance inside a surface before leaving it. Its absence is the single biggest reason skin reads as painted plastic.

inputs.means: how much of the diffuse response comes from inside rather than off the surface
how far light travels per colour channel, in millimetres of the real object. Unequal per channel is what reads as flesh rather than tinted wax.
colour of the light that comes back out, usually redder than the base colour

outputs.means: replaces the lambert term with one that wraps past the light terminator and reddens in thin areas

requires: light direction at the shading point
host_binding.binding_note: Radius is in millimetres of the real object, so a host MUST know the object's true scale. A head authored at 200mm and imported at 2 units will scatter like marble unless scale is carried.

known_losses: Screen-space and wrapped approximations lose light that enters one surface and leaves another (light through a nostril, between fingers).
Most real-time approximations ignore the direction light entered from, so hard rim lighting through thin parts is understated.

fallback.do: wrapped diffuse: wrap light ~0.3 past the terminator, plus a Fresnel rim tinted by `tint`
fallback.loses: thin-area glow and correct per-channel falloff; still removes most of the doll signal

verify: Render a sphere at 100mm with weight 0.7 and radius [2.8,1.1,0.7], lit from one side. The terminator must be soft and red-brown, not a clean grey gradient.
Backlight an ear-thickness slab. It must brighten and redden. If it darkens, transport is not bound.

name: Transmission and absorption
purpose: Light passing through: glass, resin, thin leaves, ears and nostrils against the sun.

inputs.means: how much light passes through rather than reflecting
index of refraction
what the material takes out of light over distance
distance over which that absorption happens
treat as a sheet with no interior volume: leaves, paper, cloth, ears
how much the ior varies per colour channel

outputs.means: light leaving the far side, attenuated by distance travelled

requires: ray depth or a thin-wall approximation
host_binding.binding_note: Colour must come from absorption over thickness, not from base colour. That is why real glass is green at the edge and clear at the face; base-colour glass is instantly recognisable as fake.

known_losses: Rasterised transmission cannot handle caustics or nested media.
Thin-wall mode loses refraction entirely, by definition.

fallback.do: for thin_wall only: a back-facing term driven by the dot of light direction and inverted normal, tinted by absorption_color
fallback.loses: everything volumetric; adequate for foliage, not for glass

verify: Backlight a leaf. It must go BRIGHTER than the unlit side. If it darkens, this is not bound.
A thick glass block must be clear through the faces and coloured through the edges.

name: Wear layering
purpose: Two or three complete surfaces stacked on one object — bare metal, oxide, grime — placed by where an object is worn and where dirt collects. This is what makes something look USED rather than uniformly dirtied.

inputs.means: ordered list of {response, weight, where, mask}
the placement rule for a layer
how strongly that layer covers

outputs.means: a full response per point, blended from the stack

requires: curvature and cavity maps per asset, baked once
a per-point blend of complete responses, not of channels
host_binding.binding_note: Blend COMPLETE responses, not individual channels. Lerping roughness between rust and steel produces a value that is neither, and the surface reads as a decal.

known_losses: Placement is geometric, so it cannot know history: which edge was actually gripped, where the rain ran. Those want a painted mask.

fallback.do: pick the dominant layer per point with a hard threshold rather than blending
fallback.loses: transition softness; reads as stencilled but stays honest

verify: An aged-steel object must be brightest on the edges hands touch and darkest in the cavities. If wear is even everywhere, placement is not bound.
